Fourier series. A Fourier series is an infinite sum of sines and cosines that represents a periodic function on a finite interval. Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier discovered that any periodic function, even jagged or discontinuous ones, can be decomposed into a superposition of harmonic oscillations. This insight revolutionized mathematics and physics, enabling solutions to heat diffusion, wave equations, and signal analysis. Fourier series bridge algebra, through decomposing functions, and geometry, through harmonic resonances.

Any periodic function f of x with period two pi can be written as a sum starting with a zero divided by two, then adding terms of a n cosine of n x plus b n sine of n x. The Fourier coefficients a n and b n are determined uniquely by f. Fourier coefficients are computed via orthogonality of sines and cosines. a n equals one over pi times the integral of f of x cosine of n x, and similarly for b n with sine. This orthogonality is the key to isolating each coefficient.

The series converges pointwise at continuity points. At discontinuities, it converges to the average of the left and right limits, a result known as Dirichlet convergence. This is subtle but essential for rough functions. The set of sines and cosines forms an orthonormal basis for the space of periodic functions in the sense of Hilbert spaces. This means every periodic function can be approximated arbitrarily well.

Fourier used this technique to solve the heat diffusion equation, a parabolic partial differential equation. This revolutionized applied mathematics and gave rise to the entire field of partial differential equations. The theory generalizes to non-periodic functions via the Fourier transform, an integral transform which replaces discrete frequencies with a continuous spectrum. This is core to signal processing and quantum mechanics. The Discrete Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm make Fourier analysis computationally tractable, enabling digital signal processing at gigahertz speeds.

Fourier analysis is used in audio compression like MP three, in image processing like JPEG and PNG, in medical imaging like MRI and CT scans, and in scientific instrumentation worldwide. Generalizations include wavelets and time-frequency analysis, which overcome Fourier series' limitation of poor time localization information.
